newsitem.title: GERMANY: German, French telecoms groups mull share swap.
newsitem.headline: German, French telecoms groups mull share swap.

text.p: Deutsche Telekom AG and France Telecom have begun negotiations over swapping a strategic equity stake in order to anchor their European telecommunications alliance, a Telekom official said on Friday.

Joachim Kroeske, Telekom chief finance officer, speaking to Reuters Financial Television before leaving for Paris for talks with France Telecom said he was confident the two companies would swap shares.
"An equity swap is very likely on the basis of decisions of the companies," he said. "In the long term there is no doubt."
While the two companies in the past have spoken of the option of exchanging capital, the basis for an equity swap is only now being established.
The first step was the Bonn government's decision to sell an additional 25 percent of Deutsche Telekom's capital to strategic investors over the next two years.

The second step will be the privatisation of France Telecom, which the Socialist-led government in Paris now appears to support, backing down from an election campaign pledge to block the sale of the government monopoly.
Kroeske said that in addition to talks between the companies, the German and French governments will have to agree on any swap of shares between the two companies.
It is also likely that any deal would require approval from the European Commission.

Commenting on speculation that the German and French telecoms groups could raise their joint stake in Sprint Corp of the United States, he said: "Until now we are very happy with our ten percent. Together (with France Telecom) we have a little more than 20 percent. So that's a very good position."
There has been speculation that Deutsche Telekom and France Telecom were seeking to raise their stakes in Sprint in order to be in a position to block any takeover of the U.S. long-distance company.

The German and French phone groups each hold 10 percent of Sprint and U.S. Federal Communications Commission has frowned upon the idea of allowing them to fully take over the company until French and German markets are open to competition.
This has opened the door for another company to bid for Sprint, which could put a major dent in the international strategies of Deutsche Telekom and France Telecom.
"Sprint is the core activity in our whole strategy so we have to follow if there are reactions from the other side," said Kroeske.
